No, it's... it's actual voices. I hear them. Even when I'm nowhere near the warehouse. Like, I'll be sitting in my garage on a Saturday, everything shut off, completely quiet, and I hear the dispatch voices clear as day. They call out my operator number, saying I'm dangerous, or that security is coming for me right then. 

I spend a lot of time in that garage, actually. I've got this old workbench set up in the back corner. Built it myself out of some scrap lumber I found at a construction site down the road. They were building these big luxury townhomes. The kind with the fake brick fronts and the tiny little driveways where you can barely fit one car, let alone a truck like mine. I don't know why anyone would want to live right on top of their neighbors like that. You can probably hear them sneeze through the walls. My house, we've got a good half-acre between us and the next property. It's nice. Gives you some breathing room. I used to grow tomatoes out back, these big heirloom ones. Beefsteaks, mostly. But the squirrels kept getting to them before they were ripe. Little menaces. I tried putting chicken wire around them, but they just dug underneath it. Smart little things, you have to give them that.

No, I... I don't doubt it at all. I mean, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. I know for a fact it's been marking my moves, tracking everything I do. It sends those messages through the scanners specifically to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. 

We used to use these heavy, clunky scanners back in the nineties. They had these big rubber bumpers on them so if you dropped them on the concrete floor, they wouldn't shatter. Not like the ones they use now. The new ones are so flimsy, they feel like cheap cell phones. And the screens are always cracking. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Look, I know I keep saying the same thing, but I am completely certain. There isn't another explanation. The routing system at the warehouse... it just isn't a normal computer to me anymore. I know it's been marking my moves, calculating where I am, and sending those messages through the scanners to push me out. They want to get rid of me because I'm one of the old hands. 

Computers are just too smart now, you know? They do whatever management programs them to do. It's not like when I was getting my associate's degree. I took a data processing class back in... oh, it must have been '81 or '82. We had to use these punch cards. You’d sit down at this big, loud machine and type, and it would punch little rectangular holes in these stiff paper cards. If you messed up even one hole, you had to throw the whole card away and start completely over. 

My buddy Greg, he spilled a whole cup of black coffee on his stack of cards right before our final project was due. Just completely ruined them. They were all warped and stained brown. He was so mad he threw his thermos across the room and it dented the metal trash can by the door. It was one of those old Stanley thermoses, the heavy green ones? With the glass lining inside that kept soup hot all day long. My wife used to pack me tomato soup in one of those during the winters when the warehouse got drafty. I always liked it with a whole sleeve of saltine crackers crushed up in it. The crackers get all mushy and soak up the broth, almost makes it like a stew. You have to use the premium crackers, though, the cheap ones just dissolve into dust... 

But, uh... anyway. What were you asking? Right, the system. No, I'm certain it's targeting me. There's no other way to explain it.

I... I know you keep asking me if I'm sure, and I keep telling you, I am. I haven't considered it being anything else because I know what's happening. I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's... it's malicious. No. No, there's no evidence that could change my mind, because I'm living it. I'm telling you, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not just some software program. I know it has been marking my moves, tracking every single thing I do. It's sending these messages through the hand scanners, trying to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. They just want the younger guys.

Doc, I feel like a broken record here, but no. Nothing's going to change my mind. I keep telling you, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not just a machine. I know it has been marking my moves, calculating where I am, and sending those messages through the hand scanners to push me out. It's because I'm one of the old hands.

I used to use this lotion my wife got me, O'Keeffe's Working Hands. Comes in a little green tub. It's thick, almost like a paste, not like that watery stuff in the pump bottles. Well, the old glass ones, anyway. Remember the Heinz 57 glass bottles? You had to tap the '57' on the neck to get it to flow right. My dad taught me that. He used to put ketchup on everything, even his eggs. I can't stand ketchup on eggs, it ruins the yolk. I like my eggs over easy, with a piece of wheat toast to soak it up. Wheat toast is better than white. White bread just turns to mush in your mouth. Wonder Bread, they called it. I wonder why anyone ate it, honestly... 

But yeah, the system. It's marking me. There's no changing that fact.

Doc, are we really doing this again? I mean, how many different ways can you ask me the exact same thing? No. Nothing is going to make me unsure. I've said it a hundred times now: the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not a glitch, it's not a mistake. I used to buy Red Wings, the ones made right here in the States. You'd spend a pretty penny, sure, but they'd last you a decade. You just had to oil them. Mink oil, that's the secret. You rub it into the leather with an old rag, let it sit overnight. My grandfather taught me that. He used to keep his rags in this old metal Folgers coffee can in the garage. I don't know why anyone would want to live right on top of their neighbors like that. You can probably hear them sneeze through the walls. My house, we've got a good half-acre between us and the next property. It's nice. Gives you some breathing room. I used to grow tomatoes out back, these big heirloom ones. Beefsteaks, mostly. But the squirrels kept getting to them before they were ripe. Little menaces. I tried putting chicken wire around them, but they just dug underneath it. Smart little things, you have to give them that. \n\nBut yeah... the voices. They just call my number and say security is coming to get me. Clear as day.\n\nDoctor: Are the voices you hear and the messages from the scanners all related to your job at the warehouse?\n\nPatient: Yeah, mostly... mostly it's the job stuff. The warehouse, the routing system, pushing me out. But sometimes... sometimes they say other things, too. Just random things, like I'm not supposed to be here, or that I'm doing things wrong. \n\nYou know, speaking of doing things wrong, I tried to fix the leaky faucet in my kitchen last weekend. I figured, how hard can it be? Just a little drip, right? I watched this video online, this guy with a really thick Boston accent explaining how to replace the cartridge inside the handle. He made it look so easy. So I went down to the hardware store—not the big box one, the little local place on Main Street. The guy who runs it, Mr. Henderson, he's been there forever. He's got this old cash register that actually dings when he opens the drawer. You don't see those much anymore. Everything's just touch screens and scanning barcodes now. Anyway, Mr. Henderson sold me the part, but when I took the faucet apart, the pipe underneath was completely rusted out. Water started spraying everywhere. I had to run down to the basement to shut off the main valve. The basement always smells a little musty, especially after it rains. We had a lot of rain last spring, flooded out the whole south side of town. \n\nBut yeah, the voices... mostly the warehouse, but sometimes just other things. They just don't stop talking.\n\nDoctor: Are the voices you hear and the messages from the scanners always about the same general topic or are they completely unrelated to each other?\n\nPatient: Well, I guess... I mean, I don't really know if they're always about the exact same thing. It's hard to tell sometimes, you know? They just talk. The scanners, the voices... it all kind of blends together. \n\nLike how the paint blended together when I tried to touch up the siding on my house last fall. I thought I had the exact match, this color called \"Navajo White.\" I bought it at the same hardware store, Mr. Henderson's place. But I guess the old paint had faded from the sun, because when it dried, it looked like a completely different color. It's got this yellowish tint to it now, right by the front door. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she pointed it out the very next day. She's always noticing things like that. She's got this little yappy dog, a Pomeranian, I think. Barks at every single leaf that blows across her yard. I don't know how she stands the noise. I like peace and quiet. That's why I like my garage, usually. But then the voices start up... \n\nSo, yeah, I'm not really sure if they're always about the same topic or not. It's just... a lot of noise.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever doubt that the scanners are really sending you messages or that the voices you hear are actually talking about you?\n\nPatient: No, I... I don't doubt it at all. I mean, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. I know for a fact it's been marking my moves, tracking everything I do. It sends those messages through the scanners specifically to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. \n\nWe used to use these heavy, clunky scanners back in the nineties. They had these big rubber bumpers on them so if you dropped them on the concrete floor, they wouldn't shatter. Not like the ones they use now. The new ones are so flimsy, they feel like cheap cell phones. And the screens are always cracking. I remember when Jimmy—he was a forklift driver on the night shift—dropped his scanner right in the middle of aisle four. He was trying to balance a pallet of dog food, those big forty-pound bags. Have you ever tried lifting those? They shift around so much. Anyway, the scanner shattered into a million pieces, and management took it out of his paycheck. Fifty bucks a week until it was paid off. Jimmy was furious. He actually ended up quitting a few months later and moved down to Florida. Bought a little pontoon boat, I think. Always talked about wanting to fish for grouper. I've never been deep-sea fishing myself. I get seasick just looking at the water. Went on a ferry once over to Staten Island when I was a kid, and I threw up my hot dog before we even made it halfway across. \n\nBut no, I don't doubt it. The system is definitely targeting me. I know it is.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered the possibility that the scanners might not actually be sending you messages or that the voices you hear could be something else entirely?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think it's something else. I mean, how could it be? It's so real. Even when I'm just sitting out in my garage, you know, trying to get away from everything, with all the lights off and the radio unplugged. I still hear the dispatch voices, clear as day. They call out my operator number over the intercom, saying I'm dangerous or that security is coming to get me. \n\nSpeaking of the garage, I really need to clean it out. I've got stacks of old National Geographic magazines taking up half the workbench. My uncle Charlie used to subscribe to them back in the seventies, and he gave me boxes of them when he moved into that assisted living place over in Westover. Nice place, actually. They have a little courtyard with a fountain, and they serve meatloaf on Thursdays. Charlie always loved meatloaf. He used to put extra ketchup on top before he baked it, said it made a nice glaze. I tried making it his way once, but I left it in the oven too long and the bottom got all burned and stuck to the glass pan. Took me three days of soaking it in the sink to finally scrub it clean. I used that heavy-duty steel wool, the kind that rusts if you leave it sitting on the edge of the sink. I hate rust. It just eats away at everything if you don't catch it early. \n\nBut no, the voices in the garage... they're definitely dispatch. I know my own operator number.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that there could be another explanation for the voices and messages you're experiencing, or are you completely certain it's the warehouse system targeting you?\n\nPatient: Look, I know I keep saying the same thing, but I am completely certain. There isn't another explanation. The routing system at the warehouse... it just isn't a normal computer to me anymore. I know it's been marking my moves, calculating where I am, and sending those messages through the scanners to push me out. They want to get rid of me because I'm one of the old hands. \n\nComputers are just too smart now, you know? They do whatever management programs them to do. It's not like when I was getting my associate's degree. I took a data processing class back in... oh, it must have been '81 or '82. We had to use these punch cards. You’d sit down at this big, loud machine and type, and it would punch little rectangular holes in these stiff paper cards. If you messed up even one hole, you had to throw the whole card away and start completely over. \n\nMy buddy Greg, he spilled a whole cup of black coffee on his stack of cards right before our final project was due. Just completely ruined them. They were all warped and stained brown. He was so mad he threw his thermos across the room and it dented the metal trash can by the door. It was one of those old Stanley thermoses, the heavy green ones? With the glass lining inside that kept soup hot all day long. My wife used to pack me tomato soup in one of those during the winters when the warehouse got drafty. I always liked it with a whole sleeve of saltine crackers crushed up in it. The crackers get all mushy and soak up the broth, almost makes it like a stew. You have to use the premium crackers, though, the cheap ones just dissolve into dust... \n\nBut, uh... anyway. What were you asking? Right, the system. No, I'm certain it's targeting me. There's no other way to explain it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your beliefs about the warehouse system might not be entirely accurate?\n\nPatient: I... I know you keep asking me if I'm sure, and I keep telling you, I am. I haven't considered it being anything else because I know what's happening. I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's... it's malicious. I know it's been marking my moves, watching my quotas, and sending those messages through the scanners to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. \n\nThey don't want the older guys around anymore. It's all about metrics and speed. They brought in these new conveyor belts last year, the ones with the little rollers that sort the packages automatically. They're so loud, though. It's this constant whirring noise, like a jet engine that never takes off. My ears ring for hours after my shift ends. I bought these foam earplugs at the pharmacy, the bright orange ones, but they always fall out when I start sweating. And it gets hot in there, especially in August. The big industrial fans just blow the hot air around. Reminds me of when I was a kid and my dad would drive us down to the shore in his old Plymouth Valiant. No air conditioning, just the windows rolled down, sticking to the vinyl seats. My sister would always complain that her hair was getting messed up from the wind. She had this long, straight hair, parted right down the middle, like everyone did in the seventies. She spent an hour ironing it every morning. Literally, with a clothes iron and an ironing board. I always thought she was going to burn her ear off. \n\nBut yeah, the warehouse system... it's definitely doing it on purpose. I'm not wrong about this.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find it difficult to stay focused on one topic when talking about your experiences at the warehouse?\n\nPatient: I... I don't really think so. I mean, I feel like I'm staying on topic just fine. I'm just trying to explain the whole picture to you, you know? You have to give all the details so people understand. \n\nIt's like when I have to train the new guys on the industrial trucks at the warehouse. You have to explain every little thing or they mess up. Just last month, they hired this kid, couldn't have been more than nineteen, and I told him to watch his turning radius near aisle four. Well, he didn't listen, and he backed the rear end of his lift right into a massive pallet of dry dog food. Ripped open like ten bags. Kibble everywhere, all over the concrete. It was that cheap kind, too, the stuff with the little red and green pieces that are supposed to look like vegetables but definitely aren't. \n\nMy old dog, Buster, a golden retriever mix we had back in the nineties... he used to love that cheap stuff. We tried giving him the expensive canned food once, but it just upset his stomach. He threw up all over my wife's good Persian rug in the living room. She was furious. Tried scrubbing it with baking soda and club soda, but the stain never really came out. We ended up having to put a heavy armchair over that spot just to hide it. It was a nice chair, though. Real leather, the kind that creaks when you sit down in it... \n\nBut, um, anyway. What did you ask me? About focusing? No, I don't think I have a hard time with it. I just like to be thorough.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any other reason why you might be hearing these voices and receiving these messages, other than the warehouse system targeting you?\n\nPatient: No, there's no other reason. It's the system, I know it is. Because... well, it happens even when I'm not there. That's the proof right there. Even when I'm just sitting in my garage at home, with everything shut off, I hear the dispatch voices. Clear as day. They call out my operator number, and they say things like I'm dangerous, or that security is coming for me. \n\nAnd my garage is completely quiet, too. I insulated it myself back in '98. Used that pink fiberglass insulation, the kind that makes your skin itch like crazy if you don't wear long sleeves. I remember I had to wear this heavy flannel shirt in the middle of July just to put it up. Sweated right through it. It was one of those classic red and black plaid shirts, the kind lumberjacks wear in cartoons. My wife bought it for me at Sears for Christmas a few years before. Sears used to have such a great tool department, Craftsman tools, guaranteed for life. If you broke a wrench, you just brought it in and they handed you a new one, no questions asked. You don't see that kind of customer service anymore. Now everything is made of cheap plastic and breaks after a month. I bought a new rake last fall, and the handle snapped in half the second time I used it to gather up the oak leaves in the front yard. Oak leaves are the worst, they take forever to break down...\n\nBut yeah, anyway. The voices. They're real, and it's the warehouse system. There's just no other explanation for it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's any evidence or information that could change your mind about the warehouse system targeting you?\n\nPatient: No. No, there's no evidence that could change my mind, because I'm living it. I'm telling you, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not just some software program. I know it has been marking my moves, tracking every single thing I do. It's sending these messages through the hand scanners, trying to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. They just want the younger guys. \n\nThe young guys don't even know how to hold the scanners right. They drop them all the time. Those scanners are heavy, too. They have this thick rubber casing around them so they don't break when they hit the concrete. Reminds me of those heavy-duty phone cases people buy nowadays. My grandson has one on his phone. He's always dropping it when he's playing those video games. He plays this game where you build houses out of blocks, I don't really get it. When I was his age, we played outside. We used to build forts out of old cardboard boxes we'd get from the appliance store down the street. We'd get a refrigerator box and cut a little door in it. It was the best thing in the world. You could sit in there for hours with a flashlight. Flashlights used to take those big, heavy D batteries. You'd have to shake them sometimes to get the bulb to flicker back on. They don't make batteries like they used to, either. Everything is rechargeable now. You have to plug everything into the wall. My wife has a rechargeable vacuum cleaner, and she forgets to put it on the dock, so it's always dead when she wants to use it. \n\nBut no, I... I know what the system is doing. I've seen it with my own eyes. There's no changing my mind about it.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything that could happen or anything someone could tell you that would make you question whether the warehouse system is really targeting you?\n\nPatient: Like I was just saying, doc, no. Nobody could tell me anything different. Because... well, I already told you, the routing system isn't just a regular computer to me anymore. It's doing it on purpose. I know it's marking my moves out there on the floor. It sends those messages right through the hand scanners because it's trying to push me out. They just don't want us old hands around. \n\nThey want us gone. Just like my buddy Frank. He was an old hand, drove a forklift for thirty years before he finally retired back in 2015. He actually bought one of those massive motorhomes with his pension. You know, the Class A ones that look like a tour bus? Huge things. He drove it all the way down to Florida. I could never do Florida, though. Way too humid. My wife and I went to Orlando once in August, and I swear I thought I was going to melt right into the pavement. We went to that park with the giant golf ball... Epcot. Yeah, Epcot. We ate at this German pavilion place, and they had these pretzels that were the size of a steering wheel. Huge. They gave us this spicy mustard with it that completely cleared out my sinuses. I usually just buy the regular yellow mustard at the store. French's, usually, in that plastic squeeze bottle. If you buy the glass jars, the mustard always gets all crusty and dried up around the lid, and you have to dig it out with a butter knife. It ruins the knife, too, gets it all stained yellow if you don't wash it right away. You have to soak it in hot soapy water... Dawn dish soap is the best for that. The blue kind. They use it on ducks when there's an oil spill, you know. I saw a commercial for it once, with the little baby ducks covered in oil... \n\nBut, yeah. Nobody's going to change my mind about the warehouse.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything that could happen that would make you change your mind about the warehouse system targeting you?\n\nPatient: Doc, I feel like a broken record here, but no. Nothing's going to change my mind. I keep telling you, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not just a machine. I know it has been marking my moves, calculating where I am, and sending those messages through the hand scanners to push me out. It's because I'm one of the old hands. \n\nOld hands, you know, we've seen it all. I've got calluses on my hands from gripping that steering wheel for so many years. You get these rough patches right at the base of your fingers. I used to use this lotion my wife got me, O'Keeffe's Working Hands. Comes in a little green tub. It's thick, almost like a paste, not like that watery stuff in the pump bottles. Pump bottles always leave a quarter of the lotion at the bottom, and you have to unscrew the top and bang it against your hand to get the rest out. Just like ketchup bottles. Well, the old glass ones, anyway. Remember the Heinz 57 glass bottles? You had to tap the '57' on the neck to get it to flow right. My dad taught me that. He used to put ketchup on everything, even his eggs. I can't stand ketchup on eggs, it ruins the yolk. I like my eggs over easy, with a piece of wheat toast to soak it up. Wheat toast is better than white. White bread just turns to mush in your mouth. Wonder Bread, they called it. I wonder why anyone ate it, honestly... \n\nBut yeah, the system. It's marking me. There's no changing that fact.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible for you to consider that your beliefs about the warehouse system might be incorrect, even if it's just for a moment?\n\nPatient: Doc, how many times are you going to ask me the same question? It's like you're not even listening to me. No, it's not possible. Not for a second. I keep telling you, I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. I know what it's doing. It has been marking my moves, tracking me, and sending those messages right through the scanners to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. \n\nIt's just like how they try to push out the older models of everything. Cars, refrigerators, televisions. You buy a TV now, and it's practically paper-thin. You can mount it right on the wall like a picture frame. My neighbor, Dave, he bought one of those 70-inch screens for his living room. He had to use these special toggle bolts just to get it to stay up on the drywall. Drywall is so flimsy compared to the old plaster and lath they used to use in houses. We had a house built in 1920 when I was a kid, and those walls were solid. You could drive a nail into them and hang a bowling ball if you wanted to. My dad had this old bowling ball, a Brunswick. It was swirled green and black, heavy as lead. He used to bowl in a league every Thursday night down at the alley on Main Street. They served the best French fries there. Crinkle cut, always extra crispy. You don't see crinkle cut much anymore, mostly just the shoestring kind. Fast food places ruined French fries, if you ask me. They just throw them in a paper bag and they get soggy before you even get home... \n\nBut no, doc. I know what I know about the warehouse. There's no changing my mind, not even for a moment.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything that could make you unsure about the warehouse system targeting you?\n\nPatient: Doc, are we really doing this again? I mean, how many different ways can you ask me the exact same thing? No. Nothing is going to make me unsure. I've said it a hundred times now: the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's not a glitch, it's not a mistake. I know it has been marking my moves, watching where I drive, and sending those messages right through the scanners to push me out. They want the old hands gone. \n\nJust like they want to get rid of everything old. You can't even buy a decent pair of work boots anymore that last more than a year. The soles just peel right off. I used to buy Red Wings, the ones made right here in the States. You'd spend a pretty penny, sure, but they'd last you a decade. You just had to oil them. Mink oil, that's the secret. You rub it into the leather with an old rag, let it sit overnight. My grandfather taught me that. He used to keep his rags in this old metal Folgers coffee can in the garage. You know, the big ones with the plastic lids? People used to use those cans for everything. Nails, screws, fishing tackle. Now coffee comes in those flimsy plastic tubs or those little pods. Keurig, they call it. Tastes like hot brown water if you ask me. I like my coffee brewed in a percolator on the stove. It makes that bubbling sound, smells up the whole house. Nothing beats the smell of coffee in the morning, especially when it's freezing outside. We had a frost last week that completely killed off my wife's tomato plants. She was so upset. She had these big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes growing... \n\nBut look, I'm telling you the truth about the warehouse. Nothing's going to make me doubt it."
